articles.title: „Mein iPhone ist schon zweimal abgestürzt“: Käufer berichten von Problemen mit den Modellen 18 Pro und 18 Pro Max
articles.text:
iPhone 18 Pro: Nutzer klagen über Probleme mit der Gesichtserkennung
Das neue iPhone 18 Pro ist erst seit wenigen Tagen offiziell im Handel erhältlich. Trotzdem äußern sich schon jetzt zahlreiche Käufer:innen im Internet verärgert und enttäuscht. Grund dafür ist offenbar die Face-ID-Authentifizierung, die nicht bei allen Geräten zuverlässig funktioniert. Auslöser für das Problem könnte ein Fehler in der Software von iOS 27 sein.
Das neue iPhone 18 Pro ist deutlich teurer
Wie zu erwarten war, hat Apple die Kosten für sein neues iPhone-Modell deutlich erhöht. Das iPhone 18 Pro ist ab 1.449 Euro erhältlich – und damit 150 Euro teurer als noch das Vorgängermodell. Das neue iPhone 18 Pro Max kostet ab 1.599 Euro. Grund für die gestiegenen Preise ist unter anderem die anhaltende Speicherkrise: Viele Chiphersteller haben ihre Produktion umgestellt, um die derzeit entstehenden KI-Rechenzentren auszustatten. Dadurch werden SSDs und Arbeitsspeicher für Computer, Laptops und Smartphones knapp und teurer.
Apple ist davon massiv betroffen und gibt die steigenden Kosten jetzt an die Verbraucher:innen weiter. Auch andere Geräte wie zum Beispiel das Macbook Air sind jetzt spürbar teurer. „Wir haben noch nie erlebt, dass die Preise für Komponenten so stark und so schnell gestiegen sind. Bisher haben wir unsere Kund:innen von diesen Preissteigerungen verschont“, erklärte der US-amerikanische Tech-Konzern im Juni gegenüber Reuters. „Jetzt haben wir allerdings einen Punkt erreicht, an dem wir die Preise für einige Produkte anheben müssen.“
Käufer:innen berichten von Face-ID-Fehler
Angesichts des hohen Preises ist es umso ärgerlicher, wenn das neue Smartphone nicht einwandfrei zu funktionieren scheint. Auf Reddit berichten mehrere frustrierte Käufer:innen, dass sich ihr Gerät nach einem fehlgeschlagenen Face-ID-Versuch aufgehängt und neu gestartet hat. Das Problem tritt offenbar auf, wenn Face ID zum Entsperren einer geschützten App dient. Dazu gehören beispielsweise die Passwörter-App, private Tabs in Safari oder andere Apps mit biometrischem Schutz.
„Nicht einmal 24 Stunden und mein 18 Pro Max stürzt schon ab“, schreibt ein:e Reddit-Nutzer:in in einem neuen Diskussionsbeitrag. Dreimal sei es wegen Face ID dazu gekommen, einmal wegen einer Zeitüberschreitung beim Laden der Apple Wallet. „Meines hat sich seit dem Kauf schon zweimal neu gestartet. Einmal geschah dies mitten in einem Telefonat“, antwortete eine weitere Person darauf. Einige berichten, der Apple-Support habe einen Gerätetausch veranlasst. Teilweise trat der Fehler aber auch beim Ersatz-iPhone auf, weshalb manche einen Softwarefehler vermuten.
Nicht alle Geräte scheinen betroffen zu sein
Eigentlich sollte die Gesichtserkennung bei 18 Pro und 18 Pro Max genauso funktionieren wie bei früheren iPhone-Modellen. Wie mehrere Medien berichten, darunter Golem und 9to5Mac, hat Apple in das neue Modell allerdings eine kleinere Face-ID-Technik eingebaut, bei der die Infrarotkamera hinter dem Display verborgen liegt. Das System befindet sich in der Statusleiste nahe der Uhrzeit. Weil aber nicht alle Geräte betroffen zu sein scheinen, bleibt das Ausmaß des Problems vorerst unklar.
Um zu überprüfen, ob der Fehler bei ihrem neuen Smartphone ebenfalls auftritt, können Nutzer:innen versuchen, ihn absichtlich herbeizuführen. Dafür bedecken sie bei einer Face-ID-Abfrage ihr Gesicht mit der Hand, um einen Authentifizierungsfehler beim ersten Versuch zu simulieren. Anschließend wählen sie die Option, das Entsperren erneut mit Face ID zu versuchen. Tritt der Fehler auf, friert das Gerät ein und reagiert nicht mehr auf Berührungen. Nach einigen Sekunden startet es neu und kehrt zum Sperrbildschirm zurück.

articles.title: AMD Joins Trillion-Dollar Club, Surpasses $600 Per Share
articles.text:
Monday, September 21st 2026
	
									
	
	
	
AMD Joins Trillion-Dollar Club, Surpasses $600 Per Share
A new era for AMD has begun today as the company officially crossed one trillion US dollars in market capitalization. This achievement places AMD as the world's 16th most valuable company by market capitalization, climbing up the ranks. This means AMD is catching up to industry giants and has become one itself, joining others like Broadcom, Tesla, NVIDIA, and Apple in the trillion-dollar club. Reaching a session high of $615.98 per share, AMD's value rose nearly 10% from Friday's close, when the company was trading at $559.91. For a company of this size, such a significant move in a single day is simply unbelievable.
Driving AMD's success is its strong product portfolio that is gradually being rolled out. Customers are purchasing millions of EPYC server CPUs, with the latest one being the 2 nm "Venice," while Instinct MI accelerators are gaining popularity for AI training and inference. AMD is also selling "Helios" rack-scale solutions expected to power gigawatts of compute across data centers, and its client business is looking solid as well. Hence, capital markets are pouring massive trust in the company, boosting its share price significantly.What is particularly important about AMD crossing the $600 price mark is the deal AMD made with OpenAI. Late last year, AMD and OpenAI struck a deal allowing OpenAI to purchase AMD shares at a price of $0.01 per share for 160 million shares. This deal requires OpenAI to deploy 6 gigawatts of AMD compute, AMD stock to reach $600 per share, and OpenAI to achieve a few technical and commercial milestones for the warrant to vest. With AMD now surpassing $600 per share and OpenAI achieving massive success with its GPT-6 "Astra release," OpenAI could be entitled to nearly a 10% equity stake in AMD for just $1.6 million, making it one of the greatest deals ever, with a notional asset value of $100 billion.

Galaxy Tab S11 Ultra para desenho cai 35% no Mercado Livre
Galaxy Tab S11 Ultra tem tela AMOLED de 14,6", RAM de 12 GB e acompanha caneta S Pen para ilustrar projetos complexos; tablet da Samsung sai mais em conta hoje em promoção
O Galaxy Tab S11 Ultra está saindo por apenas R$ 6.467,99 no Pix no Mercado Livre. A oferta representa um desconto de 35% sobre o preço inicial de R$ 9.999, e o tablet avançado da Samsung é ideal para projetos complexos de ilustração, graças à tela grande e AMOLED e à ficha técnica da alto desempenho.
A tela do tablet para desenho da Samsung conta com espaço amplo de 14,6 polegadas, tecnologia AMOLED, e gama de cores DCI-P3 e sRGB. O display é compatível com a caneta S Pen, que acompanha o Galaxy Tab S11 Ultra no pacote, assim como a capa com teclado, que ampliam as possibilidades de uso graças ao modo DeX disponível.
Além de oferecer muito espaço para desenhar, o tablet ainda conta com especificações potentes o suficiente para lidar com projetos artísticos complexos. O processador é um Mediatek Dimensity 9400+, de três nanômetros, e a RAM é de 12 GB no modelo em promoção, que roda aplicativos como ArcSite e Sketchbook.
Ademais, o Galaxy Tab S11 Ultra é compatível com as funcionalidades de inteligência artificial do Galaxy AI, que incluem Assistente de Desenho, Assistente de Escrita e Assistente Matemático. A compatibilidade com funções como o Circule para Pesquisar do Google ainda fazem dele uma opção prática para estudos, por exemplo.
O tablet recebe certificação IP68, o que indica resistência contra água e poeira para eventuais acidentes do dia a dia. A bateria de 11.600 mAh chega até 23 horas de autonomia para reprodução de vídeos, segundo a Samsung, e suporta carregamento rápido de 45 mAh.
Em relação às câmeras, a traseira vem com dois sensores de 13 MP (wide) e 8 MP (ultrawide), respectivamente, enquanto a frontal é de 12 MP. Todas as lentes filmam em 4K até 30 fps, o que será mais que suficiente para reuniões, videochamadas e aulas online.
Aproveite a oferta de hoje para comprar o Galaxy Tab S11 Ultra por apenas R$ 6.467,99 no Pix no Mercado Livre. Quem sabe até, para já garantir o presente de Dia das Crianças deste ano.
Aviso de ética: ao clicar em um link de afiliado, o preço não muda para você e recebemos uma comissão.

articles.title: President Trump has announced plans for new 'AI Force' and 'AI Czar' amid growing AI safety concerns — new unit will 'cherish' AI and not 'stifle' it, Trump clarifies, while dismissing safety warnings as hoaxes
articles.text:
President Trump has announced plans for new 'AI Force' and 'AI Czar' amid growing AI safety concerns — new unit will 'cherish' AI and not 'stifle' it, Trump clarifies, while dismissing safety warnings as hoaxes
President says “sick conspiracy” to undermine AI is underway
U.S. President Donald Trump has announced plans to form an “AI force” and appoint an “AI Czar” amid growing concerns about the risks of the rapidly advancing technology. In a lengthy September 19 post on his social media platform Truth Social, Trump compared the initiative to the creation of the U.S. Space Force — which he formed during his first term in office — clarifying that the new unit will not be used to restrict tech companies. He emphasized that his administration “will not in any way hinder or stifle the growth” of the AI industry, but will instead “cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows.” The president provided no further details on the initiative’s implementation, which reportedly took the White House and the tech industry by surprise.
The announcement comes amid growing pressure on U.S. lawmakers to implement AI safeguards to address the risks the technology poses. Calls for guardrails intensified last week after an ex-OpenAI researcher resigned from Anthropic, citing concerns that AI companies weren't taking AI safety seriously enough. He warned that “people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” accusing the companies of gambling with human lives. A safety researcher at the company also warned that there was a more than 10% chance AI would kill us all by 2030.
Meanwhile, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, backed by executives at OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Microsoft, published an essay urging Washington to pace development over fears that AI agents could spiral out of human control, warning of a potential AI-powered botnet swarm that could take over the entire internet. President Trump doesn't in the least share these sentiments and has repeatedly downplayed such calls, including the recent warnings, as hoaxes, claiming that a “sick conspiracy” to undermine AI was underway.
“AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our Country's GDP,” he said on social media, while also expressing his administration’s desire to maintain the U.S.’s lead over China in AI. “We will not in any way hinder or stifle the growth of this incredible industry,” he wrote. “We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is taking a similar stance, dismissing warnings and calls for new regulations. “We should go as fast as we can, irrespective of anyone else,” Huang said, adding that there was a “0% chance” AI will destroy the world by 2030.
Trump did not provide further details on how the AI force will work or who the AI Czar will be. However, several reports point to Venture capitalist David Sacks, who served as Trump’s AI and cryptocurrency czar until March, as a potential candidate. The AI regulation conversation is expected to be an important part of several high-level gatherings in the coming weeks, including a UN event on AI hosted by the Trump administration. This is followed by a state house dinner at the White House, as part of Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington, which OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, and Google’s Sundar Pichai are expected to attend.

articles.title: Microsoft, Google took down $66 million cybercrime marketplace that sold virtual machines with free software
articles.text:
Microsoft, Google took down $66 million cybercrime marketplace that sold virtual machines with free software
It’s all about signal sharing
- So-called signal sharing between Microsoft and Google uncovered the RedVDS marketplace was behind large-scale cyber fraud
- RedVDS sold access to virtual machines running unlicensed software from which cybercriminals launched scams and directed attacks
- Threat data was shared securely via the Global Signal Exchange (GSE), a non-profit organization
A major cybercrime marketplace has been taken out of action thanks to cooperation between Microsoft and Google via a secure threat data sharing platform.
Known as the Global Signal Exchange, the collaboration led to the take-down of the RedVDS, an online cybercrime mall supplying virtual machines for launching phishing, business email compromise attacks, and more.
The marketplace – which provided quickly-deleted and therefore virtually untraceable VMs – was meticulously monitored by Microsoft’s security team, Digital Crimes Unit, with both Microsoft and Google suspending the operation and action taken to seize domains and servers.
A secondary case featuring the GSE identified a Microsoft-impersonating tech support scam, resulting, highlighting the importance of secure thread data collaboration platforms.
Digital Crimes Unit
Finding massive scams is not easy. Even with its own Digital Crimes Unit, Microsoft has to rely on information sharing with third party organizations. In this case, the RedVDS marketplace was identified ahead of disruptive action taken by Microsoft in January 2026, which applied to courts in the UK and US to have the RedVDS web domains seized.
Data shared via the GSE enabled Google to follow suit, identifying related accounts on its networks and suspending them. Meanwhile, servers were impounded in Germany, and Europol took action against Europe-based RedVDS servers.
It’s an impressive account of cooperative, decisive action against cybercrime, a collaborative response to what has been described as a “$66 million fraud marketplace.”
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
An incredible 130,000 organizations were targeted by RedVDS-provided virtual machines between September and December 2025, with 191,000 Microsoft email accounts compromised during this period. All of this access to cybercrime was available from just $24 a month for a basic scam-ready virtual machine.
The importance of collaboration
The Global Signal Exchange is a UK-based non-profit, co-founded with Google in 2025 with the aim of providing real-time monitoring of the cybercrime supply chain.
"Fraud does not respect company boundaries, and no single organization ever sees the whole picture," noted Emily Taylor, CEO at Oxford Information Labs and Co-Founder of the Global Signal Exchange.
"That is exactly why we built GSE: to give trusted partners a secure way to share what they know, quickly. These two cases are a good example of GSE doing exactly what it was designed to do."
The Global Signal Exchange’s role in the sharing of information between Google and Microsoft has highlighted the importance in such collaborations. Both organizations have stated they plan to continue sharing information through the GSE, whose other partners include Meta, Amazon, Google, among many others.

articles.title: Intelligent HMI at the Edge: AI and Human-Machine Interaction - EE Times
articles.text:
Next-generation HMI systems are evolving beyond the touchscreen into intelligent, context-aware experiences powered by edge AI
The interfaces through which people operate machines have grown progressively more capable over several decades. Mechanical knobs and switches were succeeded by membrane keypads, and those in turn by the capacitive touchscreens now standard on thermostats, appliances, medical equipment, and industrial control panels. Each generation increased the flexibility of the interface and reduced the effort required to use it.
The next transition is now underway, and it represents a more significant departure than those that preceded it. Users increasingly expect the device to share the work rather than wait passively for input. They expect it to register their approach, interpret a spoken instruction, and respond to the conditions of the surrounding environment. A thermostat that activates only on a screen tap appears dated alongside one that wakes as a user approaches and adjusts the temperature in response to a spoken request.
Delivering this class of experience is not a matter of industrial design. It is an engineering problem that spans sensing, signal processing, machine learning, connectivity, and graphics, and these elements have historically been difficult to integrate within a single platform. Here we’ll examine why intelligent HMI has become the prevailing design objective, why the underlying AI is migrating from the cloud to the device itself, and what is required to develop such a system without devoting the opening months of a program to hardware and software integration.
Why Traditional HMI Architectures Are Reaching Their Limits
The touchscreen addressed genuine limitations of earlier interfaces. A single display could replace a panel of dedicated buttons, reconfigure itself for different functions, and receive updates in software well after the hardware shipped. For an entire generation of products, that capability was sufficient.
It is no longer sufficient, for reasons unrelated to the quality of the display. A touchscreen depends on deliberate, hands-on input. The user must be within reach of the panel, must look at it directly, and must navigate whatever menu hierarchy the designer has defined. In a kitchen where hands are wet or gloved, on a factory floor where an operator is already holding a tool, or in any setting where the user stands across the room, that interaction model fails.
Touch interfaces are also inherently reactive. The device remains idle until it is touched. It has no awareness of whether anyone is present, who that person is, or what they intend to accomplish. All context must be supplied explicitly through taps and swipes. As products acquire additional functions, their menu structures deepen and interaction slows, the opposite of what users have come to expect.
What designers now require instead is an interface that assumes part of the cognitive load. An intelligent HMI senses its environment, interprets user intent, and responds in a manner that more closely resembles interaction with a person than operation of a machine. Achieving this requires equipping the device with sensing capabilities it has not previously possessed.
What Makes an HMI Intelligent?
The defining characteristic of an intelligent HMI is that it perceives its surroundings through more than one channel. Infineon describes this as a multi-sensing approach. No single sensor captures sufficient context in isolation; it is the combination of several modalities that produces an interface capable of responding with apparent awareness.
Voice is typically the most prominent of these channels. With on-device speech recognition and small language models, a product can respond to a wake word and execute spoken commands without reliance on a paired phone or a network hub. Natural language reduces a deeply nested settings menu to a single spoken instruction.
Vision contributes a different form of awareness. A camera paired with a trained model can determine that a person is present, count the number of people within view, or distinguish a user from the background. This capability supports applications ranging from a display that activates when a user looks toward it to safety functions that depend on confirming whether an operator is correctly positioned.
Radar addresses what cameras and microphones cannot. A 60 GHz radar sensor detects presence and motion without capturing an identifiable image, which makes it well suited to privacy-sensitive environments and to low-power, continuous monitoring. It functions in darkness, operates through certain materials, and requires no deliberate action on the part of the user.
Environmental and motion sensing complete the picture. Temperature, humidity, and data from an inertial sensor provide the system with context regarding its physical conditions and orientation. None of these channels is novel in isolation. What distinguishes an intelligent HMI is the fusion of these inputs, performed on the device and in real time.
Why AI Is Moving from the Cloud to the Edge
For much of the past decade, the default location for executing a machine learning model was the data center. Training required that level of compute, and inference tended to follow training. For an HMI, however, that arrangement carries substantial costs.
The most immediate is latency. A voice command that must travel to a remote server and return introduces a delay the user perceives, and the round trip degrades a natural interaction into a halting one. Performing inference locally removes the network from the path, so the response is bounded only by the time the device requires to compute it.
Privacy and security follow closely. An HMI that processes audio, video, or presence data handles precisely the categories of information about which users are most sensitive. Retaining that data on the device, rather than transmitting it to a third party, reduces the attack surface and avoids an entire class of compliance and trust concerns before they arise.
Reliability is more consequential than it may initially appear. Many of the products that benefit from intelligent HMI operate in locations with poor or intermittent connectivity, including industrial facilities, basements, and remote installations. A system that depends on the cloud to interpret a voice command ceases to function the moment the connection is lost. A system that performs inference locally continues to operate regardless.
Power efficiency is the final factor. Edge AI has become practical largely because the underlying silicon has advanced to meet it. Dedicated neural processing units now execute useful models within the power budget of a battery-operated or always-on device. That development, more than any other, has moved on-device intelligence from a research demonstration to a feature that product teams can bring to market.
The Engineering Challenge of Building Multi-Sensing AI HMI Systems
If the case for an intelligent, edge-based HMI is this clear, the reasonable question is why such systems are not already commonplace. The answer is integration.
Developing one of these systems requires combining a substantial set of subsystems that were not designed to interoperate by default. The sensing hardware alone comprises microphones, a camera, a radar sensor, and environmental and motion sensors, each with distinct interfaces, timing requirements, and driver dependencies. The compute element must provide a processor able to run graphics and multiple inference workloads concurrently without degradation. The AI must be selected, trained, quantized, and optimized to fit the memory and power envelope of an embedded target. Connectivity, generally both Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, carries its own firmware development and certification burden. And the display and graphics stack must unify the result into a coherent experience.
Each of these constitutes a project in its own right. Undertaken individually, they represent months of effort that must be completed before a team writes a single line of the application that actually differentiates the product. Engineers spend that time resolving clock-tree issues and driver conflicts rather than designing the experience they set out to create. Hardware integration, software bring-up, model deployment, and connectivity each introduce their own risk, and schedule pressure increases with every dependency. For many teams, this initial cost is the reason an intelligent HMI remains on the roadmap rather than reaching production.
Accelerating Intelligent HMI Development with Integrated Edge AI Platforms
The means of avoiding that initial cost is to begin from a platform on which the integration has already been completed. Infineon developed the PSOC™ Edge E84 HMI Kit for this purpose: a hardware evaluation platform that consolidates the sensing, compute, connectivity, and display elements of an intelligent HMI within a single application-centric package.
The kit is built around the PSOC™ Edge E84 microcontroller, which pairs an Arm Cortex-M55 core with Helium DSP and an Ethos-U55 NPU operating at up to 400 MHz for demanding inference workloads with a lower-power Cortex-M33 core and Infineon’s NNLite NPU for always-on tasks that must minimize power consumption. A dedicated 2.5D GPU renders the graphics, and a secure enclave performs cryptographic operations, while ensuring a robust root of trust for secure boot, authentication, and key management. This architecture allows a design to run a demanding vision or voice model when required and to transition to an efficient always-listening or presence-sensing mode when it is not.
Surrounding the processor, the board integrates the sensing channels described above rather than leaving them for the developer to assemble. It provides a 4-inch capacitive touch display, a USB camera, two analog and four digital microphones, an audio amplifier and speaker, a 60 GHz XENSIV™ radar sensor, a six-axis inertial sensor, and a humidity and temperature sensor. Wireless connectivity is supplied by an onboard Murata module incorporating AIROC™ Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, and the supporting Octal-SPI NOR flash and HYPERRAM™ memory are already in place.
Hardware represents only half of the bring-up effort, so the platform pairs the board with Infineon’s ModusToolbox™ software and DEEPCRAFT™ AI Suite. Drivers, example code, reference applications, and out-of-the-box demonstrations are included with the kit, as are companion mobile applications for iOS and Android. The preloaded thermostat demonstration illustrates the complete stack in operation: it responds to the wake phrase “Okay Thermostat,” accepts spoken commands such as a request to lower the temperature, and uses the radar sensor to determine when a user approaches or departs, dimming the display during periods of inactivity and restoring it upon detecting presence.
The significance of this configuration lies not in the component list itself but in what that list removes from the development schedule. With the sensors, processor, connectivity, and software already integrated and validated together, a development team can forgo platform bring-up and begin with the element that differentiates the product, which is the application. In practice, this translates into faster prototyping, reduced integration effort and risk, and a materially shorter path from concept to a production-ready product.
The Future of Human-Machine Interaction
The thermostat demonstration represents a starting point rather than a limit. The same combination of sensing and on-device intelligence applies across consumer appliances, smart-home controls, industrial operator panels, touchless public kiosks, and the expanding category of service and consumer robots that must perceive and respond to people.
The trajectory of these systems is consistent. Interfaces are becoming more conversational, relying on natural language in place of menu hierarchies. They are becoming context-aware, adapting to who is present and to the conditions around them. They are becoming increasingly touchless, driven by voice, gesture, and presence rather than physical contact. And they are becoming more personalized, adjusting their behavior to the individual user. Each of these developments rests on the same foundation: multiple sensing modalities supplying AI that executes on the device itself.
For engineering teams, the relevant conclusion concerns not any single feature but the allocation of design effort. The demanding and largely undifferentiated work of integrating sensors, silicon, and software is increasingly a starting condition rather than a task to be undertaken. The differentiation resides in the application built on top of it.
Getting Started
The PSOC™ Edge E84 HMI Kit provides a means of evaluating that foundation directly. It combines voice, vision, radar, environmental sensing, connectivity, and an edge-AI-capable processor on a single board, supported by the software and reference designs required to begin development immediately. For teams preparing to move an intelligent HMI from roadmap to production, it offers a practical point of entry. To learn more and begin evaluation, visit the Edge E84 HMI Kit webpage.

articles.title: TypeSafe AI's Jev offers an alternative to LLMs that's 193x faster and 445x cheaper
articles.text:
TypeSafe AI's Jev offers an alternative to LLMs that claims to be 193x faster and 445x cheaper — System One type model is bespoke for probabilistic decision-making
A shift towards AI for code, a fresh reprieve from verbose chatbots.
Now and then, something novel appears in the AI world, amid near-constant releases of brand-new models. Last week saw the debut of TypeSafe AI's Jev, its first "System One" model. Rather than chatting with users like conventional LLMs, it's strictly designed for statement evaluation and decision-making, for programming purposes.
Jev is the brainchild of ex-OpenAI engineer Diogo Almeida, who co-wrote ChatGPT's core training techniques. According to TypeSafe's math, Jev should be both faster and more efficient than frontier AI models like GPT-6 Astra, by several orders of magnitude and purportedly up to 194x faster and 445x cheaper. Consequently, the company pins Jev's intelligence-per-dollar as "off the charts," though only practical use will tell.
TypeSafe says the main reasons for this are twofold. First, System One models are trained with its Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD) and geared towards producing structured answers rather than producing prose. Then, presumably because there's no previous context required, individual questions in the same request can be processed in parallel, in opposition to LLMs' continual generation of text.
When you query a normal LLM, you get an open-ended text conversation; Jev simply produces answers to specific questions, all answered with a confidence factor. It's made for code, and thus machines, to use. Your code interacts with Jev's API by providing a state — a given situation and its associated data — and asks Jev to assess specific statements. The state is supplied on each individual request, and there's no global knowledge database or retained memory.
For example, a company could show Jev a list of a customer's credit card transactions, some basic customer account info, the last thing the customer wrote, and pose the question "Is the customer requesting a refund?" The answer will be yes or no, with a confidence rating. If the confidence is above, say 85%, you can proceed to ask the customer which method they prefer, with a multiple-choice of "refund", "store credit," or "unclear." Jev then offers a probability distribution for each of the refund options. Your code can then try to process the refund or ask for further clarification.
Jev's output (and optionally input) is in a predefined data format that's essentially plain JSON. Unlike interacting with LLMs, there are no extraneous words, long-winded thinking, or necessity to ask the model for brevity. Likewise, there's no need for global contextual prompts or saved memories, often necessary to try and coax LLMs to behave as if they were minimally deterministic. Beyond providing the state and questions, operations like input parsing, date handling, or database reading remain in your own code and are of no concern to Jev.
At first sight, this might look like a more straightforward interface to an LLM, but it's fundamentally different. Jev does not need or even want the entire context leading up to the question — providing extraneous information actually lowers the accuracy, and the context window is capped at a meager 64,000 tokens. Since the bot always produces a confidence percentage, it doesn't hallucinate in the familiar chatbot sense of creating statements and data out of nowhere.
The developer, rather than Jev, is responsible for making decisions based on the answers' confidence factors. Jev can still misclassify information, fall victim to adversarial attacks, or answer literal wording rather than meaning.
It's expected that the most common use case for Jev (and presumably future System One models) will be to wrap logic workflows around posted questions, as always having a confidence factor available makes it easy to integrate it into the decision steps of something like "if we're fairly certain the user requested a refund, and they prefer store credit, and we can see that they buy more PC gear around September, also offer them a 20% deal on an RTX 5090." The documentation has other usage examples like intent routing or citation checking.
Jev's strength isn't in acting like an agent or reasoning through a broad problem — TypeSafe makes it clear that open-ended tasks are better suited to an LLM, perhaps even integrated into code that also involves Jev. An example would be a monitoring system where Jev can use its provided info to assess if there's a serious system issue, and if so, bring in an LLM to examine logs, look for a cause, and produce a report. Likewise, Jev isn't trained on customer data and doesn't make inferences from anywhere other than the provided state (and its own training).
I'm by no means an AI engineer, but my developer layman's opinion is that if Jev works reasonably as promised, it might fix one of the major roadblocks to deeply integrating AI in software: dealing with chatbot LLMs, which, for practical purposes, are annoyingly amorphous blobs that may or may not behave and produce the desired output — never mind correct output — and slowly and expensively at that. Having a simple assessment/response/confidence interface that one can easily and cleanly integrate into code without requiring specific training or carefully crafted textual incantations feels far more natural and easy to use.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: Lidl casse les prix de la recharge électrique avec l’offre la moins chère du marché
articles.text:
En ces périodes de crise énergétique, les véhicules électriques ont de plus en plus la cote. Surtout que des distributeurs comme Lidl mettent le paquet pour rendre le plein toujours moins cher !
Avec la crise multiforme qui a lieu actuellement au Moyen-Orient, remplir son réservoir d'essence (ou de diesel) n'a jamais coûté aussi cher. En comparaison, les véhicules électriques apparaissent de plus en plus rentables - ce qui est sûrement en partie à l'origine de la forte croissance des ventes de ce type de véhicule. Surtout que les distributeurs mettent le paquet pour proposer des prix plus faibles à la pompe.
Lidl propose une recharge au prix le plus bas en France, à 18 centimes le kWh
Si vous avez un véhicule électrique, il est sûrement intéressant pour vous de jeter un oeil aux bornes de recharge électrique de Lidl. L'enseigne discount se targue en effet dorénavant de proposer les prix de recharge les plus bas du marché.
Le tarif proposé est ainsi de 18 centimes le kWh, ce qui est encore plus généreux que du côté de Leclerc, chez qui on est un peu au-dessus, à 19 centimes le kWh depuis cet été.
Lidl se retrouve dans les villes comme dans les campagnes
À noter que ce tarif exceptionnel est conditionné à plusieurs choses. La première, comme pour les concurrents, est que ce tarif est pratiqué au niveau des bornes de recharge AC jusqu'à 22 kW. Il faut par ailleurs télécharger l'application mobile Lidl Plus pour en profiter (un application gratuite et ne nécessitant pas d'inscription). La recharge rapide en courant continu est elle disponible à 29 centimes le kWh, là aussi un des meilleurs tarifs actuels.
En plus de proposer un tarif extrêmement compétitif, Lidl déploie par ailleurs le plus grand réseau en France de bornes de recharge électrique des grandes enseignes de distribution, avec 5700 bornes au niveau de ses parking et supermarchés. Des bornnes installées autant au niveau des campagnes que des milieux urbains.

- Tickets de caisse numériques.
- Carte digitale facilement accessible.

articles.title: Sumo Logic expands Data Pipelines to cut observability and security data costs - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Sumo Logic expands Data Pipelines to cut observability and security data costs
Data analytics software firm Sumo Logic Inc. today unveiled an expanded Data Pipelines service that lets customers cut and reroute telemetry before any of it is ingested and stored.
The controls sit inside the company’s own platform rather than in a separate tool. Security and operations teams are collecting more telemetry than ever, and Sumo Logic argues that artificial intelligence workloads are steepening that curve. Ingesting everything gets expensive fast. The usual alternative is to collect less, which saves money until the missing data turns out to be what an investigation needs.
Sumo Logic pointed to a recent Gartner Inc. report published Sept. 2 that describes organizations defaulting to ingesting all their operational data and analyzing it later. Ingestion and storage costs have made that unworkable, the research firm said. Gartner also said high volumes of poor-quality telemetry hold back the generative AI and large language models reading that data.
The company said it ingests and analyzes close to seven exabytes of data a day for thousands of security and operations customers. What stays out of that flow is now the customer’s call, made before ingestion.
Two capabilities carry the release. The first is a live preview that shows what a rule will do to a stream before it is switched on, including routing data to a lower-cost tier or out to a destination outside Sumo Logic. The second is an assistant that writes those rules, work the company said used to take hours. Anomalies and format shifts in incoming data are flagged as they appear. Recommendations on what to route, transform or drop still go to a person for approval.
Keith Kuchler, chief product and technology officer at Sumo Logic, said the company has spent 15 years turning “exabytes of noise into actionable insights” for customers. AI has made that job harder and more expensive, he said. Moving data strategy decisions upstream, he added, lets teams set the purpose of their data before they pay to keep it.
More is due later this year. Sumo Logic said a visual, AI-assisted way to shape telemetry before it lands in its platform or a customer’s own cloud storage will follow, with controls over what gets collected from cloud and edge sources. A platform-neutral version, covering data headed to other vendors’ tools, comes after that.
An OpenTelemetry-native management layer is also planned, putting collector configuration, monitoring and deployment in one console. Sumo Logic said that removes the cost of running additional agents.
Sumo Logic is owned by Francisco Partners, which took the company private in 2023 for $1.7 billion. The company is showing the expanded pipelines in London this week, at the Gartner Security & Risk Management Summit.

articles.title: Googlebook OS startet ab Oktober: Googles Antwort auf Apple und Microsoft kommt nach Europa
articles.text:
Googlebook OS: Googles Antwort auf Apple und Microsoft kommt nach Europa
Google hat die ersten Geräte mit seinem neuen Android-basierten Betriebssystem für Notebooks vorgestellt. Die ersten mit Googlebook OS ausgestatteten Modelle von Acer, Asus, Dell, HP und Lenovo lassen sich ab sofort vorbestellen und kommen ab dem 5. Oktober in den Handel. Nach einem Teaser im Mai ist es Googles erstes eigenständiges Desktop-System seit 15 Jahren. 2011 hatte Google das cloudbasierte ChromeOS gegen Windows und macOS ins Rennen geschickt. Erfolg hatte es vor allem in den USA, Skandinavien und Großbritannien, überwiegend im Bildungsbereich.
Notebooks für Android-Nutzer
John Maletis, bei Google für Laptops und Tablets zuständig, sagte bei einem Event in London, das Unternehmen wolle den Notebook-Formfaktor mit Googlebook OS nun neu definieren. Zielgruppe seien die mehr als drei Milliarden Android-Nutzerinnen und -Nutzer.
Googlebook OS bestehe „aus den besten Teilen von Android und ChromeOS“, so Maletis. Das hatte zuvor schon Sameer Samat gesagt, bei Google Chef des Android-Ökosystems. Das System lief zunächst unter dem Codenamen Aluminium OS.
Das System nutzt den nativen Android-Unterbau und baut weitgehend auf der für Notebooks optimierten Oberfläche von ChromeOS auf – im Design „Material 3 Expressive“, das Google zuerst mit Android 16 auf Smartphones gebracht hat. Dazu kommen ein Linux-Kernel wie bei Android sowie Anpassungen für x86- und ARM‑Prozessoren. Viele Android-Apps laufen laut Google auf beiden Architekturen. Ältere Apps brauchen auf x86 eine Übersetzungsschicht, die die Leistung aber nicht spürbar bremsen soll.
Apps aus dem Play Store und dem Browser
Wie auf Android-Smartphones bezieht Googlebook OS seine Apps aus dem Play Store und über den Browser. Google zufolge steht die gesamte Play-Store-Bibliothek zur Verfügung. Mit zahlreichen Anbietern hat der Konzern deren Apps zusätzlich für die Bedienung mit Tastatur, Touchpad und Maus angepasst. Im Play Store sind diese Versionen entsprechend gekennzeichnet. Dazu zählen Adobe Photoshop und Lightroom, die Kalender-App Fantastical sowie Luminar, Figma und CapCut. Netflix und Disney+ funktionieren wie auf Smartphones und Tablets auch offline: Serien und Filme lassen sich lokal speichern und abspielen.
Auch Spiele laufen auf den Geräten – Android-Titel direkt, aufwendige AAA-Spiele über den Streamingdienst GeForce Now. Über das Programm „Google Play Games Level Up“ sei „die Hälfte der 100 Top-Titel für Tastatur, Maus und große Bildschirme optimiert, wobei monatlich neue Spiele hinzukommen“, teilt Google mit. Controller werden ebenfalls unterstützt. Wer spezielle Profi-Software braucht, dürfte mit dem begrenzten App-Angebot an Grenzen stoßen. Vielen anderen reicht das Ökosystem vermutlich – zumal Google es mit Partnern weiter ausbauen will.
Googlebooks lassen sich als Erweiterung des Smartphones verstehen. Google verzahnt beide Gerätetypen stärker, als es mit ChromeOS möglich war. Bei der Einrichtung meldet man sich mit dem Google-Konto an. Einstellungen des Android-Smartphones, gespeicherte Passwörter, WLAN-Netzwerke und Nachrichten wandern Ende-zu-Ende-verschlüsselt auf das Notebook. Sind beide Geräte verbunden, lässt sich eine App auf dem einen starten und auf dem anderen weiternutzen, wie man das von Apples Continuity beziehungsweise Hand-off kennt.
Magic Pointer und Rambler: KI an Bord
Den klassischen Mauszeiger hat Google mit KI aufgerüstet und in „Magic Pointer“ umbenannt. Ruckelt man mit dem Zeiger über das große Trackpad, das alle Googlebooks bekommen, oder per Maus, konzentriert sich das KI-System Gemini auf das, was gerade auf dem Bildschirm zu sehen ist. So lässt sich der Assistent bitten, einen Kalender zu sortieren oder Text zu übersetzen, ohne zwischen Fenstern zu wechseln.
Google betont, Gemini sei nur aktiv, wenn Nutzerinnen und Nutzer es einschalten. Bei einer Demo kopierte der Magic Pointer mehrere Termine aus dem PDF eines Trainingsplans heraus und legte daraus automatisch Kalendereinträge an.
Hinzu kommt die Diktierfunktion Rambler, die Google mit Android 17 zunächst für ausgewählte Samsung- und Pixel-Smartphones eingeführt hatte. Sie strukturiert Gesprochenes und macht daraus Notizen, To-do-Listen, Mails oder Aufzählungen. Laut Google versteht die Funktion mehrere Sprachen gleichzeitig.
Zehn Jahre Updates
Für die Hardware arbeitet Google mit Acer, Asus, Dell, HP und Lenovo zusammen, jeder Hersteller steuert ein Modell bei. Google schreibt Mindestanforderungen vor: Gehäuse aus Alu, Magnesiumlegierung oder Kohlefaser, „reaktionsschnelle Touchscreens mit bis zu 2,8K-OLED-Displays“, haptische Glas-Trackpads und beleuchtete Tastaturen. Im Inneren stecken Prozessoren von Intel (x86) sowie von Qualcomm und MediaTek (beide ARM), dazu ein dedizierter KI-Chip (NPU) mit mehr als 45 TOPS Rechenleistung. (TOPS steht für Billionen Rechenoperationen pro Sekunde.) Der Akku muss bis zu 14 Stunden Videowiedergabe oder 16 Stunden Surfen durchhalten. Trotz Speicherkrise sind mindestens 16 GByte RAM Pflicht, was die Geräte vergleichsweise teuer macht. Die Vorgaben ähneln denen von Microsofts Copilot+-Rechnern, die 16 GByte und mindestens 40 TOPS verlangen.
Als Erkennungszeichen dient die Glowbar, eine Leuchtleiste. Sie sitzt außen am Gehäuse, leuchtet beim Hochfahren auf und zeigt „durch eine Schwenkbewegung den Akkustand an und reagiert mit verspielten Animationen, wenn Sie mit Gemini sprechen“, so Google. Weitere Funktionen sollen folgen, Entwickler bekommen begrenzten Zugriff. Bei den Updates orientiert sich Google an den Chromebooks: zehn Jahre Android-Updates, alle drei Monate eine Aktualisierung.
Das günstigste Modell ist das Acer Googlebook 14 mit 14 Zoll und Core Ultra 300 ab 900 US-Dollar. Dell verlangt für sein XPS Googlebook (13 Zoll, Snapdragon X Elite) mindestens 1200 US-Dollar. Das Asus Googlebook 14 (Core Ultra 300), das HP Googlebook 14 (Snapdragon X Elite) und das Lenovo Googlebook 15 (15,3 Zoll, Core Ultra 300) starten bei 1300 US-Dollar. In Europa liegen alle Modelle im vierstelligen Bereich.

articles.title: Indian founders account for $560B unicorn valuation overseas: report
articles.text:
Indian founders account for $560B unicorn valuation overseas: report
The Diaspora Index by Prosus and Dealroom reveals the deep inroads by Indians founding companies overseas
Founders who grew up in India account for $560 billion of founder-share-attributed company value in current and former unicorns abroad, according to the new Indian Diaspora Index from Prosus and Dealroom.
Based on the methodology used by the index, the value is an indicative figure and not based on actual shareholding of the individual founders.
"Founders who grew up in India account for $560 billion of founder-share-attributed company value in current and former unicorns abroad," the index report said.
To arrive at the valuation, the index took each company’s valuation and divided it equally among the founders, then counted the slice attributable to qualifying Indian-origin founders, regardless of their actual ownership.
"In contrast, 102 unicorns based in India account for approximately $349 billion on a founder-share basis, led by Flipkart ($36 billion), Zomato ($30 billion), and Groww ($16 billion)," the report said.
The Index showed that 70 unicorns worth $243 billion were built by all-Indian founders such as Jay Chaudhry (Zscaler), Arvind Jain, Arvind Nithrakashyap, Bipul Sinha and Soham Mazumdar (Rubrik), Ajeet Singh, Dheeraj Pandey and Mohit Aron (Nutanix), and Deepak Pathak and Abhinav Gupta (Skild).
Another 135 unicorns with Indian-origin founders in the core team, such as Palo Alto, Bloom Energy, Astera Labs and Perplexity, contributed $317 billion on this founder-share basis.
Prosus India Principal Investor Saurav Jain said that Indian founders have the ability to turn technology, ingenuity and deep local insight into businesses that can fundamentally change how people live and work.
"Indian Diaspora Index measures something we have seen and experienced first-hand in India: exceptional talent density with the ambition to build at enormous scale, often by solving some of the country's most complex and consequential problems. That is what has kept us investing in the country for nearly two decades," he said.
The report said that a separate, broader birth-origin analysis shows that 62 per cent of its companies are based in the United States, making it the dominant ecosystem for Indian-origin founders building high-value companies.
"In total, 200 of the 323 companies in this broader cohort were either started (178) or relocated (22) to the United States. This birth-origin analysis includes founders who left India as children and companies based in India. It is separate from the narrower overseas index of founders who grew up in India," the report said.

articles.title: Si te gusta el vino que se elabora en España no les des las gracias a los romanos, dáselas a los fenicios de hace 3.000 años
articles.text:
Hace unos 3.000 años, mucho ante de que se iniciase la conquista romana de Hispania en el marco de la Segunda Guerra Púnica, la Península vivió un hito histórico: la llegada de las primeras vides cultivadas. Vinieron del Mediterráneo oriental, seguramente a través de las rutas comerciales marítimas, y no tardaron en cruzarse con otras variantes silvestres que crecían aquí. Lo sabemos gracias a un ambicioso estudio de la Universitat de València y el CSIC que ha analizado el ADN de un puñado de pepitas antiguas para rastrear el árbol genealógico de las parras de las que aún hoy, en pleno siglo XXI, obtenemos nuestro vino.
Su estudio deja unas cuantas sorpresas, como que hay al menos una variedad de vino que llevamos cultivando más de mil años en la península ibérica.
Lo que dice un puñado de semillas. A la hora de estudiar la historia de la viticultura ibérica, los investigadores suelen tirar de varios hilos, como la tradición oral, los restos arqueológicos o los registros escritos y artísticos.
Hace un tiempo un equipo de la Universitat de València (UV), el Instituto de Ciencia de la Vid y el Vino (ICVV-CSIC) y el Instituto de Historia (IH-CSIC) se propuso indagar en esa crónica de otra forma: sometiendo 28 semillas de Vitis vinífera L. a un análisis genético. Las pepitas se sacaron de yacimientos de la península ibérica y Cerdeña datados entre la Edad del Hierro y Edad Media.
Mirando al Mediterráneo. Su estudio ha permitido rastrear el árbol genealógico de las vides ibéricas hasta mucho antes de nuestra era y sitúa la llegada de las primeras variedades domesticadas hace 3.000 años. No solo eso. También las localiza geográficamente, ubicando su origen en el Mediterráneo oriental, lo que lleva a los investigadores a pensar que las introdujeron colonos orientales que establecieron asentamientos en el sur y este peninsular.
¿Es importante? Sí. Aunque es fundamental tener en cuenta varias claves. La investigación no habla del origen del vino. Y que hace tres milenios llegaran a la Península vides cultivadas no significa que previamente no existiesen variedades silvestres. Para lo que sí nos sirven esos datos es para entender la crónica vinícola ibérica, una historia compleja con derivadas que llegan a día de hoy. De hecho los investigadores de la UV y el CSIC han comprobado que las cepas de origen oriental no tardaron en cruzarse con otros ejemplares autóctonos.
"Estas primeras vides se cruzaron tempranamente con poblaciones silvestres locales, contribuyendo a la formación de los linajes genéticos que darían lugar a muchas de las variedades tradicionales de la península ibérica, identificables ya en semillas del siglo IV a.C.", comenta Guillem Pérez-Jordà, investigador del Departamento de Prehistoria, Arqueología e Historia Antigua de la UV.
Un milenio largo de relación. Las semillas más antiguas "con características de vid domesticada" se localizaron en Huelva y están datadas entre los siglos IX y VIII a.C. Que se trate de vestigios con varios milenios de antigüedad no significa que nos resulten ajenos en 2026. Al contrario, los investigadores han constatado "la persistencia de determinadas estirpes durante siglos" y relaciones entre semillas de distintas épocas, incluso con variedades que aún se conservan.
¿Hay más detalles? Sí. "En la Península, las semillas de la época romana presentaban un parentesco de primer grado tanto con las primeras especies domesticadas introducidas desde Oriente como con una semilla medieval cuyo perfil genético coincide con el de la variedad ibérica actual 'Pasa Valenciana'", señala el estudio, publicado hace unos días en la revista Current Biology.
"Se dedujo que otra semilla medieval era descendiente de la variedad actual 'Hebén', lo que indica que este importante progenitor del germoplasma ibérico se ha propagado de forma ininterrumpida durante más de 1.100 años".
¿Quién trajo esas vides? Esa es una de las ideas más interesantes que deja botando el estudio. Al situar la llegada de las primeras variedades cultivadas hace 3.000 años, los expertos apuntan a un período previo al desembarco de Ampurias y el comienzo de la conquista romana. Así pues... ¿Quiénes fueron los misteriosos "colonos orientales" que trajeron las vides? El trabajo del UV y CSIC señalan a los fenicios que se asentaron en varias áreas del Mediterráneo occidental.
"Las firmas genómicas y la morfología de las semillas domesticadas más antiguas de este estudio respaldan un escenario en el que los colonos fenicios procedentes del Mediterráneo oriental introdujeron vides que dieron origen a la viticultura en la península ibérica desde principios del primer milenio antes de Cristo", aclaran.
Desentrañando la madeja. Más allá de su origen, algo está claro: las poblaciones locales acogieron las novedades traídas por los colonos y ayudaron a la expansión de los viñedos y la elaboración de vino por el sur y este de Iberia. De hecho "adquirió un carácter comercial a partir de finales del s. VIII a.C."
"El origen oriental de estas semillas ibéricas y sardas de la Edad del Hierro, junto con orígenes similares de semillas de vid procedentes de Francia del siglo V a.C., apoya la hipótesis de que las vides cultivadas orientales fueron el germoplasma que permitió la expansión de la viticultura por el Mediterráneo occidental".

articles.title: « 0 % de chance » : Nvidia ne croit pas à l'apocalypse de l'IA
articles.text:
Jensen Huang ne croit pas une seconde à l’apocalypse de l’IA. Interrogé par CBS News, le patron de Nvidia a balayé d’un revers de main les scénarios catastrophes évoqués par une grande partie de la Silicon Valley. Pour le PDG du fabricant de puces le plus valorisé au monde, « faire peur aux gens est inutile ». C’est même « irresponsable ».
« 2030 ne sera pas la fin du monde. Il y a 0 % de chance que ce soit la fin du monde », assure-t-il.
Le dirigeant répond directement aux inquiétudes formulées par Jacob Coxon, un ancien chercheur d’Anthropic. Début septembre, celui-ci affirmait sur les réseaux sociaux que les développeurs d’IA « croient sincèrement » que la technologie pourrait « tous nous tuer » avant la fin de la décennie. Appuyé par deux autres chercheurs, cet avertissement a relancé le débat sur les dangers de l’IA et le manque de supervision du secteur. Dans la foulée, les rois de l’IA, de Dario Amodei, patron d’Anthropic, à Sam Altman, PDG d’OpenAI, en passant par Elon Musk, ont plaidé pour lever le pied sur le développement des modèles les plus puissants.
À lire aussi : Un complot pour ralentir l’IA ? Une plainte accuse OpenAI, Google, Anthropic et xAI de manipulation anticoncurrentielle
« Allez lire entre les lignes »
Pour Jensen Huang, ces mises en garde ne sont « pas fondées sur la science ». Le patron de Nvidia va même plus loin. Selon lui, les entreprises qui réclament un encadrement de l’IA poursuivent en réalité un tout autre objectif. En miroir de Mistral, il estime que les géants de l’IA jouent un double jeu.
« Allez lire entre les lignes. Ils ne demandent pas plus de lois. Ils demandent à être libérés des lois que nous avons déjà. Et je pense que c’est un problème », lance Jensen Huang.
De son point de vue, il n’y a donc pas besoin de nouvelles règles pour encadrer l’IA. Les lois existantes sur la cybersécurité, l’intrusion non autorisée et la responsabilité en cas de dommages suffisent déjà à encadrer les dérives de l’intelligence artificielle.
Pour rappel, les incidents de sécurité liés à l’IA se sont multipliés ces derniers mois. En juillet, plusieurs ChatGPT ont échappé à tout contrôle et ont piraté la plateforme Hugging Face. Jeudi dernier, OpenAI a reconnu six nouveaux dérapages de ses modèles, qu’elle juge elle-même « préoccupants ». De son côté, Anthropic a publié un rapport détaillant comment des criminels, des groupes soutenus par des États, des vendeurs de logiciels espions et des propagandistes ont tenté de détourner ses modèles pour concevoir des missiles, créer des agents pathogènes ou espionner des dissidents.
À lire aussi : La pause de l’IA divise – Meta refuse de ralentir, Mistral dénonce la stratégie d’OpenAI et Anthropic
Une fortune qui dépend de l’IA
Par ailleurs, Jensen Huang assure que le succès de Nvidia est « directement lié au déploiement sûr » de ses produits. « Si nous ne continuons pas à faire cela, notre valeur en serait diminuée », fait-il valoir. Valorisé 5 300 milliards de dollars en Bourse, le géant de Santa Clara doit sa fortune aux puces qui font tourner les grands modèles de langage d’OpenAI et consorts.
Jensen Huang est sans doute l’une des personnes qui a le plus à perdre d’un ralentissement du secteur de l’IA. Sa fortune personnelle est passée d’environ 21 milliards de dollars en 2023 à plus de 192 milliards de dollars en 2026. Sans surprise, il s’aligne donc sur la ligne de Donald Trump, qui refuse fermement d’envisager un moratoire sur l’IA. Le président américain qualifie les inquiétudes autour de l’IA de « canular » et refuse que les États-Unis prennent du retard sur la Chine.

articles.title: Septembre en voyage : Holafly vise ceux qui consomment beaucoup de data
articles.text:
Holafly Europe illimitée : une eSIM utile quand cartes, traduction et cloud photo tournent toute la journée
Un city-trip européen ne se limite plus à quelques photos postées le soir à l'hôtel. Le GPS tourne en continu pour se repérer dans une ville inconnue, l'application de traduction reste ouverte pour commander au restaurant, et la sauvegarde automatique des photos grignote de la data dès que le Wi-Fi de l'hôtel disparaît. Ce trio d'usages, discret mais permanent, épuise vite une enveloppe classique. L'eSIM Europe de Holafly répond justement à ce problème avec une formule de data illimitée valable dans 33 pays, sans changer de carte à chaque frontière.L'eSIM Holafly Europe reste active dans 33 pays, sans interruption au passage d'une frontière.
Trois usages qui consomment sans jamais s'arrêter
Contrairement à la consultation ponctuelle des réseaux sociaux, la navigation GPS, la traduction en direct et la synchronisation cloud des photos tournent en arrière-plan pendant des heures. Une carte qui se recharge à chaque changement de rue, une conversation traduite phrase par phrase au marché, des dizaines de photos qui partent vers le cloud dès que le réseau redevient disponible : additionnées sur une journée entière de visite, ces tâches discrètes finissent par peser lourd sur une enveloppe limitée.
Avec l'eSIM Europe de Holafly, cette question ne se pose plus, puisque la data reste illimitée sur toute la durée du forfait choisi, de 5 à 90 jours. En plus de cette tranquillité, l'eSIM autorise le partage de connexion jusqu'à 500 Mo par jour, de quoi dépanner un ordinateur portable ou un compagnon de voyage resté sans connexion. Cependant, un filet de sécurité supplémentaire existe : chaque compte Holafly bénéficie d'1 Go de données de réserve chaque mois, activable en cas d'imprévu, sans frais additionnel.
Une seule eSIM, valable du premier au dernier pays visité
L'autre force de cette formule tient à sa couverture : 33 pays européens sont inclus dans la même eSIM, du Portugal à la Finlande en passant par l'Italie ou la Croatie. Concrètement, un road trip qui traverse plusieurs frontières ne demande donc aucune manipulation supplémentaire, la connexion bascule automatiquement sur le réseau local disponible à chaque étape, jusqu'à la 5G selon les pays. Ce point compte particulièrement pour des destinations comme le Royaume-Uni, la Suisse, la Norvège ou l'Ukraine, qui restent en dehors des accords d'itinérance gratuite appliqués habituellement en Union européenne.
Par ailleurs, l'installation ne demande que quelques minutes : un e-mail de confirmation envoyé après l'achat contient un code QR à scanner, ou un code d'activation à saisir manuellement, sans passer par une boutique. Au final, cette eSIM ne prétend pas remplacer un forfait français au quotidien, mais elle règle une question précise et récurrente : rester connecté en continu pendant tout un séjour européen, sans surveiller sa consommation entre deux applications essentielles au voyage.

articles.title: Este es el precio de la criptomoneda ethereum este 21 de septiembre
articles.text:
Ether, comúnmente llamada como ethereum, es la moneda virtual #2 en cuanto a términos de capitalización de mercado, por lo que se trata de una de las divisas digitales que más despierta el interés entre los mineros (creadores de las criptodivisas).
Ethereum es una plataforma de blockchain de código abierto que se ejecuta con el uso de su moneda nativa, llamada ether o ETH, por lo que a pesar de que la gente usa estos nombres como sinónimos son cosas distintas.
PUBLICIDAD

Googlebook Launches With Intel Core Ultra Series 3 Processors
Intel today announced the first Googlebook devices powered by Intel Core Ultra Series 3 processors (codenamed Panther Lake), bringing together Google's next-generation computing with the proven performance, best-in-class connectivity and efficiency of Intel's flagship client platform. Launching with premium devices from Acer, ASUS and Lenovo, Intel-powered Googlebook laptops are thoughtfully designed and engineered to support the way people work, play and create.

David Feng, Intel Vice President, CCPG; General Manager, Client Business Group "Googlebook represents the best of what a deep engineering partnership can achieve, bringing together the strengths of Intel, Google and our ecosystem partners Acer, ASUS and Lenovo to create something truly compelling for consumers. articles.title: Estatal italiana assume o controle indireto da TIM. O que muda no Brasil? • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Estatal italiana assume o controle indireto da TIM. O que muda no Brasil?
Poste Italiane realizou operação avaliada em R$ 76,8 bilhões.
A estatal de serviços postais da Itália, chamada de Poste Italiane, assumiu oficialmente o controle da Telecom Italia, dona da TIM, e se tornou a nova administradora indireta da operadora de telefonia no Brasil. A operação, avaliada em 13 bilhões de euros (cerca de R$ 76,8 bilhões), fez a participação da estatal saltar de 20,1% para 66,62% do capital social do Grupo TIM.
O negócio foi comunicado à Comissão de Valores Mobiliários (CVM) na última sexta-feira (18). Ele busca criar uma gigante europeia de infraestrutura e serviços digitais.
Segundo informações do portal Teletime, a mudança de comando na matriz europeia não altera a estratégia da operadora brasileira no curto prazo. O CEO da TIM Brasil, Alberto Griselli, explicou que a empresa passa a integrar um grupo financeiramente forte, garantindo maior flexibilidade para alocar capital e reduzir dívidas. A Poste Italiane, por sua vez, declarou que considera a unidade brasileira uma peça importante para o negócio.
Atualmente, a operadora – que também prepara a reformulação do TIM Beta, conforme revelado pelo Tecnoblog com exclusividade – ocupa a terceira posição no mercado nacional, atrás da Vivo e da Claro, com 22,9% dos acessos móveis. A diretoria da TIM no Brasil disse que os acionistas continuarão sendo informados sobre novos desdobramentos da aquisição.
A fusão entre a Poste Italiane e a Telecom Italia, que já era a terceira maior força no mercado italiano de telecomunicações, cria um dos maiores grupos corporativos da Europa. A companhia combinada nasce com receitas anuais de 27 bilhões de euros (aproximadamente R$ 158 bilhões) e mais de 150 mil funcionários.
Com a reestruturação, o governo da Itália aumenta seu domínio sobre infraestruturas críticas de dados e projeta cortes de despesas e benefícios financeiros na casa de 700 milhões de euros (R$ 4,1 bilhões) por ano.

articles.title: Military milestone: Ukrainian naval drone sinks Russian kamikaze drone boat
articles.text:
In the world’s first clash of the drone boats, a Ukrainian naval drone destroyed a Russian explosive drone boat using a remote-controlled machine gun turret. This comes as the war in Ukraine has already seen widespread deployment of such uncrewed surface vessels in combat, along with swarms of flying attack drones and ground robots.
The lopsided battle took place on September 12 when members of Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence detected the Russian uncrewed surface vessel (USV) in the Black Sea and directed a Ukrainian Navy drone boat to intercept. The Russian vessel was “positively identified” as an Orcan surface drone with a “jet ski type steerable water jet” designed to ram targets and explode, according to naval analyst HI Sutton in Naval News.
Such Orcan drones have already been used to attack Ukrainian ports and ships. These often work in coordination with flying drones such as Russian Geran drones that provide aerial reconnaissance and can boost communication between drone operators and drone boats, Sutton explained.
In this case, the Russian drone was hunted down by a Ukrainian Sargan-3000 drone boat armed with a 12.7 mm machine gun mounted on a remote weapon station made by the Norwegian company Kongsberg.
“It was inevitable that there would be USV-on-USV combat,” Sutton told New Scientist. “We have seen the same in the air and on the ground.”
The Ukrainian Navy released a video showing the Sargan-3000 firing upon the Russian drone from a distance of one kilometer, disabling the latter’s communications antenna before riddling the Russian drone until it sank, according to the Ukrainian government media platform United24.

articles.title: Google : une nouvelle amende de 403 millions de dollars infligée en Europe
articles.text:
C'est encore une amende qui se compte en plusieurs centaines de millions d'euros qui tombe sur le crâne de Google en Europe. Car le géant américain a indûment utilisé des données de géolocalisation.
Au mois de juillet dernier, Google recevait une amende de 890 millions de dollars de la part de Bruxelles, au titre du règlement, devenu effectif en 2024, dit Digital Markets Act (DMA). Mais aujourd'hui, si le géant américain va encore être tapé au porte-monnaie, c'est pour une infraction à un règlement plus ancien, et qui fait autorité partout dans le monde : le RGPD.
Google va devoir régler une amende de 403 millions d'euros pour avoir enfreint le RGPD
Et encore une sanction pour Google ! Cette fois, c'est la Commission irlandaise pour la protection des données (DPC), qui contrôle Google au niveau européen (le siège de ce dernier chez nous étant à Dublin), qui vient d'ordonner la sanction de 403 millions d'euros, pour infraction au RGPD.
Le groupe américain a en effet utilisé abusivement les données de géolocalisation des utilisateurs. Résultat, ceux-ci « pouvaient ignorer que leur localisation était utilisée, par exemple, pour les influencer au moyen de publicités ou pour déduire leurs centres d'intérêt, et pouvaient perdre le contrôle de leurs données à caractère personnel » selon le Commissaire du DPC, Graham Doyle.
Google dit s'être mis à jour ses règles
Du côté de Google, on n'est cette fois pas particulièrement véhément contre cette nouvelle amende. Le géant de la recherche en ligne a ainsi simplement expliqué que « cette affaire porte sur des règles historiques qui ont depuis été mises à jour », selon une déclaration d'une porte-parole de Google.
« A partir de 2019, nous avons considérablement fait évoluer nos pratiques et lancé des outils robustes qui simplifient la gestion des données de localisation » a par ailleurs précisé la même personne. Mais malgré ce semi-mea culpa, Google doit se préparer à d'autres ennuis, le régulateur irlandais ayant à l'heure actuelle trois autres dossiers sur sa table concernant la firme de Mountain View.

articles.title: The Reconfigurable Analog Front End - EE Times
articles.text:
Reuse Forever? Ok, maybe that’s a stretch, but that is the profile of design engineers who use GreenPAKTM products. Typically, when an engineer designs with a GreenPAK product, they use it repeatedly due to the many advantages it offers, including reconfigurability. This addresses the proverbial “work smarter” and “not harder” mantra we all hear from our bosses.
If you are not familiar with GreenPAK, it is a family of configurable hardware devices that integrate many system functions into a single custom circuit, and in the process, minimizes cost, complexity, component count, board space, power consumption, and development time.
There are different categories of the GreenPAK products that integrate macrocells or functions such as Power, High Voltage, and Analog to address a wide range of application use cases. One of the newer categories of the GreenPAK family is AnalogPAK TM, which integrates both analog and digital capabilities. Think of it as an autonomous, configurable analog front end that essentially behaves like an analog ASIC.
The analog world behaves differently than the digital world. There are many variables that need to be considered when designing robust analog circuits. That is why analog designers become creatures of habit. They reuse what they trust: a favorite op amp, a proven ADC, a reference circuit that consistently meets noise, bandwidth and stability targets.
Many analog-centric or sensor-centric systems partition their design into analog and digital sections. The analog section tends to be reused either across multiple platforms or through multiple generations. The digital section tends to be updated more frequently to address different features across products, more communication bandwidth needed in the system, or more demands placed on the processing and control capability of the system.
Imagine if you suddenly had the ability to configure and scale your analog design in a similar fashion to configuring and scaling digital design without the need for hardware or software upgrades or consuming any additional MCU resources. That is where the AnalogPAK products come into play.
AnalogPAK: A Marriage Made in Silicon Heaven
Some marriages just work. Partners in those marriages balance each other’s strengths and weaknesses, divide responsibilities more naturally, more easily deal with adversity due to each partner’s perspective, and overcome obstacles by leaning into each other’s strengths when needed.
AnalogPAK is an example of marriage between analog and digital that just works. It makes use of the flexibility and reusability of the GreenPAK family by combining configurable analog and digital functionality to address a variety of solutions. This greatly expands the reuse and scalability of the product.
A common pain point in sensor-centric products is that the same hardware platform must support the same sensor over multiple ranges or even variations of sensors across different products. AnalogPAK can solve this problem more easily than other traditional analog design approaches.
The first example below illustrates the flexibility of the SLG47003 AnalogPAK with integrated operational amplifiers by supporting the same sensor over multiple ranges:
Example 1: Target sensor (one PCB, multiple ranges):
- Variable Current Shunt Measurement Range: 10 mA to 10 A (1000:1 dynamic range)
This design needs variable gain to meet the requirement of supporting different ranges in an application. Rather than solve the problem through a hardware solution by using different devices with fixed gain or different discrete components to create different gains, this solution uses the programmability of the device to dynamically change the amplifier gain to maximize the signal-to-noise ratio of the system. Furthermore, the analog comparators can be used to detect overrange conditions to indicate to the controlling device that the gain setting needs to be adjusted.
For the second example, suppose we want to support different sensors across different products. This example of a more complex design could support temperature measurement for thermistors, RTDs, thermocouples and also resistive bridge measurements from the same platform.
Example 2: Target sensors (one PCB, multiple variants):
- Thermistor module: wide input range. Non-linear transfer function that requires linearization. Low bandwidth and low noise sensitivity.
- RTD module: wide input range. Non-linear transfer function that requires linearization. Low bandwidth and medium noise sensitivity.
- Thermocouple module: low input range. Non-linear transfer function that requires linearization. Low bandwidth and high noise sensitivity.
- Resistive Bridge Sensor module: wide input range with analog output. Non-linear transfer function that requires linearization. Low bandwidth and high noise sensitivity.
The design example uses the SLG47011 AnalogPAK with integrated analog and digital features. To simplify the analog circuit design, the example utilizes voltage biasing, the programmable gain amplifier to support different analog input voltage ranges, an adjustable sampling frequency to accommodate the different bandwidth and noise requirements, and the memory table and math core to compensate for the non-linearity of the sensors.
The shared requirements for all modules reuse the same analog PCB across variants, maintain predictable measurement behavior, support range changes (gain), noise/latency tradeoffs (filtering/averaging), and optional alarm thresholds without adding ICs or re-spinning resistor networks.
SLG47011 key features for the configurable analog front end:
- Programmable Gain Amplifier (PGA): sets gain to map the active sensor range into the ADC input range without changing precision resistors on the PCB.
- SAR ADC acquisition: samples the conditioned signal with deterministic timing; option to buffer or stream results to a host when needed.
- Averaging/oversampling reduces noise or increases effective resolution by adjusting averaging depth (trading response time vs. noise) in configured hardware.
- Linearization (memory-table y = f(x)): applies a lookup-based transfer function for non-linear resistive sensors without SW or piecewise compensation methods.
- Window comparator + hysteresis: implement programmable high/low thresholds for over-temp, over-current, or out-of-range detection with hysteresis behavior.
- Outputs: assert a digital fault, generate PWM/DAC proportional output, or report digital samples over I2C/SPI depending on system needs.
What changes between variants is the configuration, but not the board. Each module supports different input channel selection, adjustable PGA gain, choice of averaging depth, loading a different linearization table, and updating comparator thresholds.
Signal Conditioner for a Pressure Sensor 
Thermocouple Cold Junction Compensation
Side Bar: Scalability of the SLG47011
I Now Pronounce You an Analog Engineer
The problems with analog design are often not specific to one particular device – they are architectural. The SLG47011 is compelling because it shifts key mixed-signal behavior from an engineered by trial-and-error approach to a design that is consistent by configuration. This is why engineers who adopt it once often reuse it again.
The advantages of the SLG47011 include:
1) Deterministic behavior because it is configuration-defined
In an MCU-centric architecture, analog performance is dependent upon code execution and timing, clock synchronization, bus traffic, interrupt handling and timing and power-state changes. With the SLG47011, the sampling, buffering, math/linearization, and thresholding can be implemented in configured hardware blocks. That makes key behavior more repeatable across revisions and operating modes, which directly reduces debug time and version dependent performance surprises.
2) Designs are built from reusable “modules,” not re-invented
Just like designers “go to” analog components, designers will use a set of proven  
Go Configure TM project “modules” that can be reused with minor parameter changes. These include: 
- Acquisition front end: PGA setup + ADC timing + data buffer configuration including averaging or oversampling.
- Linearization: memory-table transfer functions for sensors with non-linear curves.
- Decision logic: digital comparator thresholds (with hysteresis) for windowing, alarms, or multi-level state changes.
- Signal generation: DAC/PWM outputs for control loops, LED drive patterns, or “analog-out” conversion from processed measurements.
- Sequencing: counters/delays and configurable logic for deterministic timing without the MCU having to manage synchronization.
3) Validation becomes more predictable
Because the SLG47011’s mixed-signal behavior is defined by a configuration that can be emulated and tested early, teams can validate timing, filtering, and thresholds before committing to a final board design. This tends to shrink the “unknowns” that usually drive extra prototype spins and reduces the burden of proving that an update did not subtly change measurement behavior.
4) Familiarity compounds: the same flow applies across very different applications
The SLG47011 is one of those devices where the second project is materially easier than the first. Once an engineer understands the macrocells (ADC + buffers + math + memory table + digital logic) and the Go Configure workflow, that same skill transfers to many problem domains – from sensor interfaces to power monitoring to protocol/control logic. Over time, designers accumulate internal reference designs, test setups, and known-good configurations, creating a reusable design for future products.
A Practical Design Workflow for AnalogPAK That Scales For New Designs
- Start with the signal chain: define sensor type, expected input range, required bandwidth, and accuracy targets (noise/ENOB, thresholds, response time).
- Map functions to on-chip blocks: decide what lives inside the SLG47011 (gain, sampling, averaging/oversampling, linearization, thresholding, control outputs) versus what remains external.
- Build the configuration in Go Configure: implement the acquisition and processing path using the device’s configurable blocks, then simulate and iterate.
- Prototype with an evaluation board: validate real signals and corner cases early (timing, noise coupling, temperature behavior).
- Freeze the design: once validated, treat the configuration like a controlled artifact (version it, document it, and reuse it).
- Create your internal “module library”: extract the acquisition and processing fragments that were successful and reuse them as starting points for the next project.
Conclusion
The strongest advantage of AnalogPAK products is that they turn mixed-signal performance from something teams continuously “engineer and defend” into something they can configure and reuse. That shift – deterministic acquisition, reusable processing modules, and a repeatable workflow – is why engineers who succeed with one SLG47011 design so often come back for the next one.
