articles.title: Your AI agent is burning tokens on choices that don't need words
articles.text:
Your AI agent is burning tokens on choices that don’t need words
AI agents spend a ridiculous amount of compute generating text nobody actually needs. The decisions an agent makes along the way don’t require a written answer and yet, agents still send them to generative models, wait for an answer while burning through tokens and then parse that output back. The overhead is already drawing scrutiny — OpenAI’s own researchers recently disclosed spending $7,000 a day running agent workloads.
Kev, a new family of open decision models built on Qwen 3.5, takes a different approach and skips the generation entirely.
Developer Jared Palmer released a new generation of Kev on Sunday, with 0.8 billion, 4 billion, and 9 billion parameter models built on Qwen 3.5. Kev is prefill-only, processing the state, questions, and candidates in a single forward pass before reading the decisions from a pointer head without an autoregressive decoding loop.
Kev, a new family of open decision models built on Qwen 3.5, takes a different approach and skips the generation entirely.
Decisions without generated text
Kev supports three decision types: Noul for yes/no, Choice for selecting among candidates, and Score for ordered levels, mirroring TypeSafe’s System One API. Developers provide the state and questions, and the pointer head returns probabilities across the available candidates.
For a tool-routing decision, the output could look like this:
search: 0.82
database: 0.13
calculator: 0.05
Kev can still choose the wrong tool, but because it scores only the candidates it’s given, it can’t introduce an option that isn’t on the list.
Routing, safety checks, escalation, and ranking can then move to the decision layer, leaving larger reasoning models to handle the open-ended work.
Kev can still choose the wrong tool, but because it scores only the candidates it’s given, it can’t introduce an option that isn’t on the list.
Batching choices, one pass
Multiple decisions can also be made against the same state in a single forward pass, with a block-causal attention mask isolating the questions while the pointer head scores each set of candidates independently.
Palmer’s documentation shows the 4B model processing three questions in 277 milliseconds in bf16 on an M5, although without a controlled comparison against Qwen generating equivalent answers on the same hardware, the result doesn’t establish how much faster the approach is in practice.
The ability to evaluate several decisions against the same context could become more useful as agent loops grow more complex, but skipping generation doesn’t make the resulting decisions inherently better.
Calibration limits and tradeoffs
The largest model, Kev-9B, reached 83.7% accuracy on the project’s locked out-of-domain test, according to Palmer’s model card. That’s a developer-reported benchmark, and Palmer documents some limitations alongside it.
The probabilities Kev returns don’t always reflect how confident developers should be in the result. Palmer found that temperature calibration can drift on unseen source distributions, a problem for agents that use probability thresholds to decide whether to execute an action or escalate it, since even a high-probability choice can still be wrong.
Fine-tuning also changes some of the capabilities inherited from the underlying model. Palmer’s evaluations show declines on general-knowledge and arithmetic tests, particularly among the smaller models. That’s consistent with Kev’s more specialized role alongside a general-purpose model, although its performance in dynamic agent environments will also depend on how well it handles tools, choices, and labels it never encountered during training — and debugging agent failures often points to infrastructure rather than the model itself.
The approach predates Kev. TypeSafe introduced Jev earlier this month as part of its System One platform, using the same Noul, Choice and Score primitives, and Kev implements its /v1/systemone request and response format so applications built against the API can point to a local Kev server instead.
Open weights, open training
The biggest difference is that Palmer released Kev under Apache 2.0 with the model weights, training code, and evaluation tooling, giving developers the option to run and train it on their own infrastructure. Jev’s weights and training data aren’t public, however, which makes direct performance comparisons difficult because differences between the models can’t be isolated to architecture, size, or training.
For applications that make only a handful of bounded decisions, constrained decoding on a model that’s already running may be simpler than adding another model to the stack. Agent loops can make those decisions constantly, however, moving through routing, ranking, safety checks, tool selection, and escalation before generating much user-facing text. It’s a pattern showing up across model architectures — stripping out unnecessary computation when the task doesn’t require it.
When those steps only require a choice or probability, Kev can handle the decision directly while leaving open-ended reasoning and final responses to the larger generative model.

articles.title: The startups fixing Europe’s AI power problem | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Earlier this year, I wrote about the AI power crisis and argued that coordination now matters more than new capacity. The numbers have not improved. Research from the International Energy Agency (IEA) shows that global data centre electricity demand is projected both to roughly double, from 485 TWh in 2025 to around 950 TWh by 2030, and to grow more than four times faster than total electricity demand from all other sectors.
Much of the capacity Europe needs already exists but sits unused most of the time. Software that orchestrates existing assets unlocks that headroom years before new lines and substations can.
Following the first piece, my colleague Anna Trendewicz and I looked into who is actually building this software in Europe. We found a small group of companies working across the four efficiency layers: grid, facility, compute and software.
Grid: making existing capacity visible
Amsterdam’s Sympower and Dublin-based GridBeyond have each raised more than €70 million. Both turn data centres and industrial energy users into flexible grid assets by aggregating their demand and bidding it into balancing markets across multiple European countries.
Munich’s Entrix ranks among Germany’s more established battery storage optimisers and trades flexible capacity across day-ahead, intraday and balancing markets.
Finland’s Capalo AI runs a virtual power plant that had contracted more than 1 GW of battery storage by the end of 2025 and has since then expanded from the Nordics and Baltics into Poland and Bulgaria.
London’s Piclo operates a flexibility marketplace that connects distributed energy assets with grid operators, and Vienna’s enspired automates AI-driven trading of flexible assets across European power spot markets (Note: Future Energy Ventures is an investor in both Piclo and enspired).
None of these companies started out as a data centre specialist. Most built their platforms for industrial and renewable flexibility, which shows how new the AI-specific version of this problem still is.
Facility: the physics layer
Darmstadt-based etalytics, a spin-off from TU Darmstadt, optimises the cooling, heating and power systems inside a facility. Its etaONE platform combines AI with physics-based digital twins and model predictive control, and operators can either let it adjust set points automatically or approve its recommendation manually. Data centre customers include Equinix, Digital Realty, NTT and Telehouse.
NTT Global Data Centers cut cooling energy by 19% with the software, and Telehouse Germany cut cooling electricity by 10.4% at its Frankfurt campus, a site it already considered well optimised. Across its customer base, etalytics reports savings up to 50%.
In 2025, M12, Microsoft’s venture fund, led an €8 million extension that brought its Series A to €16 million, and etalytics opened its U.S. business this year.
For AI operators this matters beyond the energy bill. A site with a fixed grid connection can shift every kilowatt it saves on cooling to its IT load, which turns efficiency directly into sellable rack capacity without a new site or new interconnection.
Rotterdam’s Gradyent works one step beyond the fence line. Its real-time digital twin optimises district heating networks for energy companies in more than 35 European cities, and it raised €28 million in a Series B in 2025. The platform can route a data centre’s waste heat into a city’s heating grid, where it warms homes instead of being vented.
Compute: the recovery layer
Paris-based FlexAI launched in 2024 with a €28.5 million Seed round led by Alpha Intelligence Capital, Elaia and Heartcore, Bpifrance participating. Its software places AI training and inference workload across heterogeneous hardware from different vendors and clouds, so customers are not tied to a single GPU generation.
Bristol-based YellowDog schedules workloads across on-premises, hybrid and multi-cloud fleets in a similar way.
Software: the earliest innings
Model efficiency cuts energy demand before a workload reaches the rack. San Sebastián-based Multiverse Computing compresses large language models by up to 95%, using quantum-inspired tensor networks. It raised €189 million in 2025 and announced a Series C of up to €500 million in July 2026.
Pruna AI, based in Munich and Paris, and backed by EQT Ventures, has open-sourced an optimisation engine that combines pruning, quantisation and other compression methods to make models smaller and cheaper to run.
In the U.S., incumbents are already buying this layer. Nvidia acquired OctoAI in September 2024, and Red Hat agreed to buy Neural Magic two months later. Both deals show how early this sub-layer is and how quickly it is consolidating.
The interface: where the value sits
Almost none of the companies work across layers. A flexibility aggregator does not manage GPU orchestration, and a workload schedule does not see grid prices. etalytics comes closest: beyond cooling, its platform shaves peak loads and schedules on-site storage and generation against market prices, which links facility operations to the grid. No one yet connects that to compute.
The most valuable position in this stack sits at the seams, where one system makes grid, facility and compute decisions together instead of separate vendors reporting to separate budget owners. No European company holds that position today. For founders, it is the clearest and most defensible opportunity still open.
According to Stanford’s AI Index Report, the inference cost of running a model at GPT-3.5 level fell more than 280-fold between November 2022 and October 2024, mostly through efficient models and software. Yet most AI infrastructure capital still flows into physical buildout.
In the U.S., generation can theoretically at least be revived or expanded. In Europe, where grid connection takes years longer than construction, capital that ignores the software layer is betting that the connection queue clears on schedule.
The companies above show that Europe is already building the underlying technology. From an investor’s perspective, the window to back the layer that gets more out of Europe’s existing infrastructure is still open.

articles.title: Kanin Energy raises $138 million for waste heat to power development | BetaKit
articles.text:
Calgary cleantech company Kanin Energy has secured significant capital for its “energy-as-a-service” (EaaS) business.
The news: Kanin announced a $138-million CAD new equity financing round on Sept. 16. The round was led by Chicago’s S2G Investments and Canada Growth Fund (CGF), both of which supplied $50 million USD (around $69 million CAD). Capital will support the development of Kanin’s waste-heat-to-power (WHP) projects in both the US and Canada.
From the source: “Rising power prices, grid congestion, and reliability constraints are pushing industrial companies to rethink how they source power. Waste heat has largely been an underused solution,” Marisa Sweeney, a principal at S2G Investments, said in a statement on the firm’s investment. “We view this as a category with real staying power.”
The context: Kanin operates out of both Calgary and Houston, with a focus on decarbonizing industrial waste heat through WHP projects that capture high-temperature exhaust and convert it to power without creating additional emissions. With several projects in development south of the border, Kanin is operating on an “energy-as-a-service” (EaaS) business model, where customers pay for energy services rather than the infrastructure itself. Kanin says investment from S2G and the Canada Growth Fund represents a significant milestone, as the company looks to scale its EaaS business model and expand its commercial pipeline.
Final thought: A beneficiary of several Canadian accelerator programs, including Plug and Play Alberta, MaRS, Canadian Tech Accelerator, and Foresight Canada, Kanin has leveraged the support it has received from accelerators and prior investment to quickly develop its footprint in the US market. Still, recent gains have come at a price. In an exclusive with Axios, CEO and founder Janice Tran said that, under the conditions of the raise, the company had ceded control of its board to investors to get the deal over the finish line. Tran cited increased difficulty for non-AI startups to access funds and the impacts of US-Canada tariff policies as reasons for the move.
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.
Feature image courtesy Kanin Energy.

articles.title: Techie makes his own motherboard to refurbish 15-year-old HP ProLiant N40L tower server — Raspberry Pi CM5 adds NVMe and USB 3.0
articles.text:
Techie makes his own motherboard to refurbish 15-year-old HP ProLiant N40L tower server — Raspberry Pi CM5 adds NVMe and USB 3.0
Kept the original 24-pin ATX connector, too.
Nobody likes throwing away old hardware with a lot of usable parts, and most everyone loves a nice DIY electronics project. Those two things dovetailed nicely into YouTuber EastMakes' project to repurpose his ancient HP ProLiant N40L micro-server. The machine's integrated motherboard-and-SoC was far too long in the tooth, so he did the logical thing: designed his own around a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5 (CM5).
EastMakes didn't want to trash the N40L, but it had zero NVMe slots, only USB 2.0 ports, and its once-laudable power consumption figures are rather unimpressive today. Needless to say, the computing power on offer was, at lack of a better word, minimal, as even back then the onboard AMD Turion II chip barely outran a pocket calculator. Even a contemporary Raspberry Pi can outperform the original hardware on all fronts, plus use a frugal amount of watts while doing so.
The CM5 is exactly the same as a standard Raspberry Pi 5, except it doesn't have any ports and is meant to be used with external accessories that provide them. Oftentimes, budding enthusiasts will use it with its premade corresponding I/O PCB. EastMakes did start with that board, but taking advantage of the Raspberry Pi project's open-source nature, he took the original diagrams and documentation and rolled his own variation.
The tech wizard extended the board to fit the area the original ProLiant N40L used, and printed a simple plastic 3D prototype to ensure he got the port and screw-hole locations just right. From thereon, he moved onto optimizations like trimming down to just the one HDMI port, and adding a connector stack with the Ethernet port and two USB 3.0 Type-A connectors.
He also wired an NVMe slot to the PCB for a system drive, and spent some time with trace lengths to ensure they all matched, as to not come up against any timing issues. Although EastMakes didn't go as far as adding RGB lighting, he did add a little pizzazz by way of choosing a yellow-on-black finish for his new motherboard, using PCBWay's custom configurator. Boop and Reboop switches were added as well.
After he got the freshly minted PCB, he tested it, and it worked right on the first try. We do have to add that while EastMakes found this to be a positive, any grizzled greybeard knows that when a complicated project or piece of code works fine the first time, it means there's definitely a nasty bug hidden somewhere.
Nevertheless, he put it into the N40L box, and presto, it fit just right and booted just fine, and EastMakes tested USB and Ethernet connection speeds to ensure everything was up to spec. He did stop short of adding the requisite SFF-8087 port for the hard drive bay, so we venture he has plans for that later on.

Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: I really wanted to love the new Dell XPS 13, but Dell, we need to have a serious chat about your RAM choices
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Positioned as a rival to Apple's new budget-friendly MacBook Neo, the Dell XPS 13 returns for 2026 with an all-new design and lower price point. It's a bold move, and while Dell doesn't quite stick the landing, the end result is still a solid choice of laptop for anyone who prefers Windows over macOS. Battery life and display quality are great, and the all-metal chassis feels durable, if a bit less flashy than previous models. However, it falls down a little when it comes to pricing, and the base configuration is somewhat underpowered, further compounding the price issue.
Pros
- +Thin but sturdy chassis
- +Great display
- +Performance is solid (though unspectacular)
- +Strong battery life
Cons
- -Poor port selection
- -8GB of RAM in base configuration is insufficient
- -Non-US pricing situation is dire
Why you can trust TechRadar
Dell XPS 13 (2026): Two-minute review
The new Dell XPS 13 (2026) is a shift from Dell's usual modus operandi, finally bringing the premium-quality XPS line down to a more affordable space. If that sounds familiar, it's because Apple did the exact same thing earlier this year: the arrival of the MacBook Neo has shaken up the laptop market, and evidently left other manufacturers scrambling to front their own competition to Apple's new wallet-friendly MacBook.
But before I delve into how effective a frontline soldier Dell's new effort is in the never-ending battle between Windows and Mac, it's time for a brief history lesson: the lore of XPS, if you like.
Dell's XPS brand was unceremoniously killed off last year, before being suddenly resurrected at CES 2026, presumably because their executives realised that shuttering your single most iconic and well-loved brand is a bad idea (shocker, I know). But as I mentioned above, the return of XPS has seen a paradigm shift; while the Dell XPS 14 and XPS 16 are still the pricey, high-end laptops I've come to expect from the XPS lineup, the new XPS 13 is an entirely different beast.
It's still identifiably an XPS laptop, there's no denying that. From the ultra-thin chassis to the all-metal casing and minimalist logo on the lid, you'd be forgiven for thinking at first glance that this was just another premium XPS model.
But opening up the laptop betrays its more budget-conscious nature immediately; gone are the giant, edgeless touchpad and zero-spacing keyboard seen on this year's 14- and 16-inch models, replaced instead by more traditional fare. The touchpad and keyboard here wouldn't look out of place on the average Chromebook.
A peek at the spec sheet further solidifies the new XPS 13's position as a MacBook Neo rival; a lower-end hexa-core Intel Core 5 chip and only 8GB of RAM in the base model all point to this being a more sensibly priced product.
I'll dig into the performance specifics later in this review, but the good news is that the lower-spec hardware doesn't render the XPS 13 dangerously underpowered. This laptop is perfectly capable of handling everyday work, even if it's not a performant powerhouse like its bigger siblings. The battery life is also excellent, and the display is very high quality for the price point. In short, there's a lot to love here.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Unfortunately, there are a few things that hold this new breed of XPS back. The base configuration features only 8GB of RAM, which is fundamentally insufficient in the current era of Windows software, and the measly port selection may prove frustrating for some users. It's also just a bit too expensive to be considered a true rival to the MacBook Neo.
Now, it's arguable that this isn't entirely Dell's fault. The ongoing RAM crisis, spurred by skyrocketing demand for AI data center hardware, is causing the prices of all kinds of computer components to spike sharply. Shifting to 8GB of RAM in the base configuration is very likely to be a cost-saving move. Overall, I'd say that this is a pretty solid effort from Dell – just don't expect too much from it.
Dell XPS 13 (2026) review: Price & availability
- Starts at $699 / £749 / AU$1,597.20
- Student discounts help a lot
- Available worldwide
Brace yourself: this is going to be one of the longest price sections I've written for a review in a while. There's a lot to talk about here, sorry!
Apologies to our readers outside the US: the pricing of the Dell XPS 13 beyond America is pretty damn awful, to the point where I'm worried it might have already scuppered any chance of this laptop being a genuine competitor against the MacBook Neo.
In the US, the base configuration comes with a 256GB SSD, Intel Core 5 320 processor, and 8GB of RAM. It'll cost you a very reasonable $699, or $599 with a student discount – in other words, exactly the same price as the 256GB MacBook Neo.
However, I'd generally struggle a little to recommend that version. 8GB of RAM is simply substandard for running software in Windows 11 these days, especially if you plan to run multiple programs at once. Stepping up to the safer recommended 16GB of RAM (which also mandatorily bumps up the SSD to 512GB) will cost you $899, already taking us a fair bit beyond the competing MacBook Neo. Of course, there's no 16GB version of the Neo available, but it's worth noting that the 'unified memory' used by Apple's laptops is a bit more efficient than traditional laptop RAM.
Outside the US, things start to look dicey. For starters, there's no 256GB SSD configuration available in Australia, with the cheapest available models starting at £749 / AU$1,597.20 – a far less attractive prospect after accounting for exchange rates. And if you want to bump things up to 16GB of RAM, you're looking at a fairly steep £1,099 / $1,897.50. My review unit is the 8GB UK configuration with 512GB of storage, which will cost you £899 (though at the time of writing, it's already on sale for £769)
There are higher-spec models available, too, with the RAM configurable up to 32GB and the SSD up to 1TB, as well as the option to upgrade the CPU to a significantly more powerful Intel Core Ultra 7 355. This top-spec model will cost you $1,799.99 / £1,899 / $3,698.20 – and quite frankly, at that point you might be better served by opting for the more premium XPS 14. Configurations with the Core Ultra 7 processor also benefit from an upgrade to Thunderbolt 4-capable USB-C ports.
Overall, I'm not too impressed by the pricing of the Dell XPS 13, especially considering its market position as a Windows-toting rival to the MacBook Neo. There's certainly still an argument that it deserves a place among the best budget laptops (for buyers in the US, at least), but it's not the phenomenal value product I was really hoping to see when I first heard about it. Still, if you're a US shopper who wants a basic but effective laptop for work or school, it's not a terrible choice.
- Value score: 3 / 5
Dell XPS 13 (2026) review: Specs

Dell XPS 13 (2026) review: Design
- Impressively thin and light
- Premium build quality
- Port selection is feeble
Straight off the bat, despite its aggressive redesign and shift towards more conventional aesthetics, the 2026 Dell XPS 13 still feels like a premium product. I might have complained about the pricing further up in this review, but considering that the build quality remains solid regardless of which configuration you buy, I have to admit that I'm very pleased here.
The entire chassis is machined from high-grade aluminum, making it highly durable without compromising on weight. The whole thing weighs almost exactly one kilogram, and combined with the 13.4-inch display's slim bezels, it's a very portable laptop indeed.
It's also impressively thin, measuring just half an inch thick with the lid closed. The casing has rounded corners and a smooth matte finish, which is reasonably good at resisting scratches and fingerprint marks. It's available in a few different colorways, all muted metallic tones, with availability varying between regions and configurations.
The keyboard and touchpad are totally different from what we've seen on previous XPS 13 models, now trending towards functionality over style. The LED-backlit keys are reasonably spaced, comfortable to type on even for extended periods, and have a decent amount of travel despite the laptop's ultra-thin design.
They're perhaps a little spongy on full presses for my liking, with a bit of flex in the keyboard housing; something which I consider completely forgivable in a sub-$800 laptop, but might push some users towards the more premium typing experience of the XPS 14 or 16. Similarly, the touchpad has a satisfying click, but firm presses on the bottom corners feel a tiny bit flimsy – definitely not a dealbreaker for a budget laptop, but again, it gives me pause when it comes to recommending the higher-spec models.
Thankfully, some things haven't changed from previous models. The display is once again the star of the show here: a fantastic 2.5K touch panel, boasting good maximum brightness and impressive color reproduction, especially considering that the screen is the same regardless of which internal spec you opt for. If you get the cheapest configuration, you're getting plenty of bang for your buck when it comes to the display.
Looking at the rest of the physical design, it's all good without being spectacular. The speakers are integrated under thin slots on either side of the base and are reasonably loud for such a small laptop. Don't expect thumping bass here, but the volume is good without high notes sounding tinny.
The webcam is also decent, 1080p rather than the 720p resolution you'll find on many budget-conscious laptops. I've certainly seen sharper webcam footage, and the low-light performance is merely okay, but it gets the job done well for the most part. It also supports facial recognition logins via Windows Hello. The integrated microphone array is decidedly average, though, so I'd advise getting a decent headset if you plan to make regular video calls.
Lastly, we come to connectivity, which is perhaps the most mixed part of an already mixed bag. Wireless connectivity is top-notch; Wi-Fi 7 ensures speedy, lossless internet (assuming you're connected to a network that supports it!) while Bluetooth 6.0 is an exceedingly rare sight on any laptop under $1,000.
Physical connections, though? Yeah, this one's a wash. We criticised the MacBook Neo for only having two basic USB-C ports (no Thunderbolt 4 support), and it's the same case here. Granted, these are both USB 3.2, while one of the Neo's ports is a frankly pathetic USB 2, and springing for the higher-spec CPU upgrades both ports to Thunderbolt 4, but it's still just fundamentally not enough ports.
Considering that the only way to charge the XPS 13 is to use one of the only two ports available, you're down to just a single port any time it's plugged in. Power users who want to connect multiple peripherals are going to need to spend extra on a USB-C hub, and anyone who doesn't shell out for the more powerful CPU will be dealing with slower charging and data transfer speeds.
Overall, it's a well-designed laptop that feels like it should last for years, but I will be docking a point for the sheer dearth of ports. If you prefer to connect your hardware solely via wireless means, though, you should have very little to complain about here.
- Design score: 4 / 5
Dell XPS 13 (2026) review: Performance
- Decent everyday performance
- Gets a little warm under load
- 8GB RAM is simply not enough for heavier workloads
3DMark: Night Raid: 17,611; Fire Strike: 3,308; Steel Nomad: N/A; Solar Bay: N/A; Solar Bay Unlimited: N/A; Solar Bay Extreme: N/A; Solar Bay Extreme Unlimited: N/A
Geekbench 7: Multicore: 7,103; Single-core: 2,345
Cinebench 2026: Single Core: 455; Multi Core: 1,604

Total War: Warhammer III: 1080p, Medium: N/A
Total War: Warhammer III: 1800p, Ultra: N/A
Battery Life (TechRadar movie test): 16 hours and 17 minutes
I'm a big believer in setting realistic expectations, so once I learned that my XPS 13 review unit was the UK standard configuration with 8GB of RAM and the decidedly low-end Core Ultra 5 320 CPU, I immediately tempered my hopes of great performance.
Despite this, this XPS 13 performed a bit better than I'd expected overall. Performance in my everyday workloads – including web browsing, word processing, and some light image editing in GIMP – was good, with virtually no slowdown even with half a dozen Chrome tabs open and Spotify running in the background. Windows 11 generally felt snappy and responsive.
The more you start to load it down with tasks, though, the more it struggles. The simple fact is that in the current age of computer software, 8GB of RAM just isn't sufficient for more complex or varied workloads.
It was a telling moment when Apple finally relented and upgraded the minimum starting memory on the best MacBooks to 16GB rather than 8GB back in 2024; the demands of modern professionals have shifted, and I was rather upset to see that the MacBook Neo has reverted back to 8GB as standard. However, this is less of a problem for Apple, since the 'unified memory' used in MacBooks is faster and more efficient than traditional DDR laptop RAM, and the company's total control of the Mac software/hardware ecosystem makes optimizing for less memory a bit easier.
So let's break down how the XPS 13's 8GB of RAM actually performed. I'll start with the bad news: some of my tests failed to complete altogether, loading up but then aborting. I've not seen this happen in quite a while, with the 16GB industry standard evidently shielding me from such failures.
In total, the XPS 13 failed eight of our standard benchmark tests, most of which were the more demanding 3DMark graphical tests. However, I also noticed some instability in other tests; Cinebench crashed several times before I was able to get stable readings, and 3DMark also crashed once before I was even able to start running tests.
The tests that did run showed decidedly lackluster performance in 3D rendering and similar creative workloads. This isn't a laptop you'll be squeezing in a few rounds of Marvel Rivals on, though I did manage to get Slay the Spire II running fine, so perhaps some 2D indie gaming is still on the table here.
Outside of regular testing, I also tried to fire up Adobe Photoshop and Premiere Pro. Both initially loaded without crashing, but were sluggish in practice, and Photoshop ended up crashing after about five minutes of use.
The Dell XPS 13 (2026) got rather warm during the more intensive tests. The thermal exhaust is a thin slot nestled into the display hinge, and while the fans remained impressively quiet throughout my testing, the underside of the laptop did get too toasty to comfortably have it actually on your lap while running resource-intensive software. It did remain cool and near-silent during regular office work, however.
The takeaway here is that while the 8GB model of the XPS 13 is perfectly capable of handling basic everyday workloads, it just doesn't have the oomph for anything more demanding than straightforward office or schoolwork. If that's all you want to do, the budget-friendly 8GB configuration should be fine; if you've got grander designs than that, you'll need to pay extra for a more powerful model.
- Performance score: 3 / 5
Dell XPS 13 (2026) review: Battery life
Intel's third-generation Core chips are clearly putting in some work here. Although the Dell XPS 13 (2026) only has a 52Wh battery (far smaller than the batteries you'll find on many ultrabooks these days), the efficiency of this chip can't be understated; our video playback battery test saw the laptop sail comfortably past the 16-hour mark.
There are laptops that can go for longer, but at this price point, that's a very respectable effort. It outstrips the MacBook Neo by nearly three hours according to our tests. I found that even at maximum brightness, with a Bluetooth mouse and headset connected and the Windows power mode set to Balanced, it could comfortably make it through an eight-hour workday without needing a charge.
The laptop also holds charge fantastically when not in use. My partner got sick, and I had to shelve this review for a couple of weeks, during which time the XPS 13 simply sat untouched on a desk in my home office. When I finally opened it up to start my review process, it was still at 90% charge. When plugged in, it charges up to full in just under an hour (though the higher-spec model with Thunderbolt 4 ports will presumably charge faster).
My only real criticism here is that it doesn't come with a power adapter in the UK and EU. Much like Apple's approach with the MacBook Neo, this is ostensibly due to local regulations that mandate consumers' ability to buy a laptop without a charger, but come on; you could include the option to add one at checkout. I've criticized Apple for this in the past, too: it's malicious compliance, and it's simply irritating for the end user.
- Battery life score: 4.5 / 5
Should I buy the Dell XPS 13?
Scorecard
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
| Value | The UK and Australia pricing is a shame, but student discounts help a lot, and the base model is very reasonable in the US. | 3 / 5 | 
| Design | Despite a disappointing port selection, this is a well-crafted laptop that feels nicely durable and packs an excellent touch display. | 4 / 5 | 
| Performance | Decent performance in everyday tasks, but users aiming to multitask will definitely want to invest in the 16GB RAM model. | 3 / 5 | 
| Battery life | The XPS 13 can comfortably cruise through a full workday (and then some) without needing a charge. | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Total Score | The 2026 XPS 13 isn't quite the MacBook Neo-beater that Dell clearly hoped it would be, but it's still a solid pick for anyone who wants a Windows alternative to Apple's new budget MacBook. | 3.65 / 5 | 
Buy it if…
You want something ultra-portable
The impressively slim design, one-kilo total weight, and sturdy aluminum chassis all work together to make the XPS 13 an eminently portable laptop for taking on the go.
You want a premium design for a non-premium price
It looks and feels impressively high-end, even in the cheapest available configurations. While it might be a little more function-over-form than the larger XPS models, this still feels like a premium laptop.
Don't buy it if…
You want lots of ports
There are only two ports on board, and both are USB-C (without Thunderbolt 4 in our review configuration), so you'll need a USB hub if you want to connect multiple peripherals.
You want to run demanding software
While it can handle everyday work with easy, the lower-end CPU and 8GB of RAM in the base configuration simply don't offer enough juice for power users planning on aggressive multitasking or resource-intensive programs.
Dell XPS 13 (2026) review: Also consider
HP OmniBook 7 14-inch (2025)
Like the XPS 13, the OmniBook 7 is an incredibly thin and light laptop. Not only that, our reviewer was very impressed with how well it handled all kinds of workloads, and it has a superb battery life to boot. Read our full HP OmniBook 7 14-inch (2025) review.
Asus Zenbook A14
Another ultra-portable hero, the A14 offers truly staggering battery life; in fact, it’s the most enduring laptop we've tested in recent years, lasting a staggering 28 hours in our movie playback test. Its build isn’t as premium as the XPS 13’s, and its display isn’t as bright, but it’s still a capable machine. Read our full Asus Zenbook A14 review.
How I tested the Dell XPS 13 (2026)
- Tested for one week
- Used for a variety of workloads
- 8+ years of hardware testing experience
If you've read any of my other reviews, you'll already know the drill: I swapped out my daily driver (the excellent Asus Zenbook Duo 14) for the Dell XPS 13 for one full week, including the weekend.
This helps me get a proper feeling for how the laptop functions in everyday use scenarios, testing it out for a range of typical tasks including web research, writing articles, and image editing. Naturally, I also ran the laptop through our usual suite of synthetic benchmarking tests, including our looped video test for battery life.
I've been a computer hardware journalist for more than eight years, and working for TechRadar for half a decade. In that time, I've reviewed more laptops than I can remember for numerous different publications; the number is certainly in the dozens, quite likely into triple digits by now! I put every bit of experience and expertise I've gained over those years into my reviews, so you can rest assured that you're getting accurate, bias-free information.
- First reviewed: September 2026
- Read more about how we test
Christian is TechRadar’s UK-based Computing Editor. He came to us from Maximum PC magazine, where he fell in love with computer hardware and building PCs. He was a regular fixture amongst our freelance review team before making the jump to TechRadar, and can usually be found drooling over the latest high-end graphics card or gaming laptop before looking at his bank account balance and crying.
Christian is a keen campaigner for LGBTQ+ rights and the owner of a charming rescue dog named Lucy, having adopted her after he beat cancer in 2021. She keeps him fit and healthy through a combination of face-licking and long walks, and only occasionally barks at him to demand treats when he’s trying to work from home.
